Yes, the story has an appropriate balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

**Explanation:**
The story primarily unfolds as a vivid, real-time scene: Mara unlocking the door, stepping into the hallway, turning on the faucet, finding a button, and speaking into the empty house. This sensory-rich action grounds the reader in the present moment and builds quiet tension. At the same time, the author weaves in brief, efficient moments of summary and exposition—specifically the two sentences explaining that she hadn't been there in twenty years and had left with a suitcase without looking back, as well as the brief mention of the familiar shapes of the covered furniture. This minimal exposition is just enough to give emotional weight and context to the present scene without slowing down the pacing or making the narrative feel dry.
